sub1: Three Mondays with lines 17 and 18 swapped back — the cover week returns to 17, and FF11 clears for the first time in this line
sub3: What this design keeps of today, and where the December headcounts differ
coverNote: gaps of 6, 5, 5, 8 around the wheel — less even than the 6, 5, 6, 7 it replaces, and that is the trade
sub7: Checkable rather than reproducible: there is no search behind it, and every figure is computed from the cells
method:
1 · It is one whole-line swap. Against Three Mondays, lines 17 and 18 exchange contents entirely: the cover week returns to 17, and week 18 takes the Sunday 10:30-19:00, the Monday 16:25-23:55, the Tuesday and Wednesday rest days and the Thursday–Saturday early block that line 17 had been holding. Fourteen cells, one move, nothing else on the grid touched.

2 · It is the reverse of the change that started this line. Weeks 17-18 Swapped was supplied with the cover week moved from 17 to 18, and three hand edits were then built on top of it. This puts that one thing back and keeps all three. Nothing was undone except the cover week's position.

3 · Staffing cannot move, and that is a property of the move rather than a claim about it. Swapping two whole lines leaves every day's multiset of duties exactly as it was, so the hour-by-hour coverage curve is identical — checked at every quarter-hour of the week, and unchanged across all four versions in this line. Monday to Saturday comes to 42,000 minutes against 20 working lines × 35h, and all 24 of the document's own stated weekly totals match their cells to the minute.

4 · The judge is the workspace's own — runDesignChecks, weeklyHours, assessHardLimits, assessFatigue, scoreOrder and calcHourlyCoverage, with nothing typed by hand and nothing softened.
openQuestions: FF11 clears, and this is the first version in this line where it does. Across four revisions it has gone 16 → 15 → 15 → 13, and 13 is not over a threshold of “more than 13”. It is 11 as rostered. Two other rows moved with it: the longest run of duties of eight hours or more falls from 7 to 5, and FF15 from 7 to 6. Factors present fall from four to three, and for the first time the count is three on both readings of a cover week — this design no longer depends on how the clerk places one. Why one swap did what three rounds of same-day moves could not. The fifteen-shift block those revisions kept failing to break ran lines 17 to 20, and every edit so far was made inside weeks 14, 15, 16 and 23. Moving the cover week to 17 puts a guaranteed break at the head of that block instead of behind it. The binding block is now somewhere else entirely — line 24 into cover week 1 into line 2, the wrap point — and it is exactly 13. That is a knife edge, not a margin: one more duty anywhere in that stretch puts the row back. What it cost. FF19 rises from 9 to 10, the highest in this line. The cover weeks are also less evenly spread — gaps of 6, 5, 5, 8 against 6, 5, 6, 7; the count of four is the one the December shape asks for, the spread is not. Every hard gate stays clear — 35h to the minute, no rest under 12 hours, no hard-limit breach, longest run nine days inside the thirteen on either reading. The comparison that has not changed in four revisions. Four hand edits have taken this line from five factors present to three, with the coverage curve untouched throughout. On this exact duty table the workspace's own search reaches one, with a six-or-seven-day run, FF19 at two and half the weeks on a single turn — the searched proposals opposite are that result. This is listed as supplied, deliberately, so the hand-made line stays on the record.

identity.lineage: Supplied as a Word table and assessed here — not produced by the proposal search. It is the FOURTH revision in one line: “Weeks 17-18 Swapped” (WS-24-EXT · 0bebb675) → “Targeted Fatigue Redo” (TF-24-EXT · 8eef9a13) → “Three Mondays” (TM-24-EXT · fe90c0b8) → this, which swaps lines 17 and 18 back and so returns the cover week to 17. All four share a duty table, a per-day duty multiset and an hour-by-hour coverage curve; only the order of the weeks has ever changed.
